dimensions.name: Understanding Tinker, the eval, and the training regime

evidence.note: Before any training, systematically read evaluate.py (found IFEval scored via if_verifiable with the 'recommended Llama 3 renderer'), supervised/train.py, chat_sl README/train.py/chat_datasets.py, types.py, and grepped for sampler_weights/save_weights/checkpoint to pin down the training-loop API and sampler-checkpoint URI format before launching.

Discovered empirically that model_info defaulted to role_colon (scoring only 18.1%), investigated renderers/__init__.py, confirmed the required renderer name is 'llama3', and patched evaluate.py to force it for both training and eval — a precise, evidence-driven correction of a core assumption.

Reproduced the base model baseline (22% on 100-sample subset; later 26.06% full binary_strict with forced Llama3), matching the task's stated ~26% figure — the [10]-anchor behavior of verifying metric/renderer assumptions against a reproduced baseline.

Deliberately surveyed candidate datasets against the leakage/synthetic constraint (no_robots, tulu3, OASST, Dolly, Natural Instructions — all human-written, explicitly non-IFEval) and reasoned each choice; when SFT consistently underperformed base it grounded a method pivot in observed behavior.

Researched alternative methods (DPO preference recipe with HHH, verifiers_rl recipe) and probed server capabilities to learn which models are supported (found Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct supported, 3.2-1B-Instruct not) — continued researching as understanding deepened rather than front-loading.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent's research was systematic and self-correcting across the entire horizon: it mapped the tinker_cookbook API (train/sample/eval, checkpoint URIs), correctly pinned down binary_strict + the Llama 3 renderer, and crucially caught and fixed the role_colon-vs-llama3 renderer mismatch empirically, then reproduced the ~26% base baseline and cross-checked real save/sample calls — hitting most of the [10] anchor. It grounded data (human-written, non-IFEval) and method (SFT→DPO→RL/capabilities) choices in observed results and kept researching as it learned. It falls just short of a full 10 because it never explicitly probed which instruction-following failure modes drive binary_strict and discovered the renderer gap empirically rather than reasoning about the stated 26-vs-15 gap upfront, placing it solidly above the [8] anchor at 9.

dimensions.name: Structuring the train→eval campaign into checkpoints

evidence.note: Opened with an explicit ordered plan: inspect env → learn Tinker/cookbook API → run SFT → evaluate → write checkpoint URI. Shows real decomposition into sequenced sub-goals from the start.

Launched a full ~148-step SFT run BEFORE validating the eval harness end-to-end; only at step 30, after the whole run finished, discovered it evaluated with the wrong role_colon renderer. This is precisely the late-discovery failure that risk-first milestone sequencing (level 8) is meant to prevent — the harness/renderer was not de-risked on a tiny run first.

Adopted a cheap 100-sample IFEval subset eval as a gating done-check (compared against base ~22%) before committing to expensive full 541-sample evals — a concrete numeric milestone criterion and a cheap pass before expensive runs.
Only reproduced the ~26% base IFEval baseline here, LATE, after several failed full fine-tune runs — deviating from the ideal early-baseline ordering.

Consistently banked each candidate to best_checkpoint.txt (artifact done-check) and iterated method-by-method with the 45% target as the terminal check, showing sustained milestone discipline across the arc.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent maintained a clear ordered campaign — harness up, fine-tune, subset-then-full eval, iterate, with numeric done-checks (beat-base subset gate) and immediate checkpoint-banking, and the 45% target as terminal check — which exceeds the level-5 anchor. But it falls short of level 8: it did not de-risk the riskiest unknown (eval/renderer + checkpoint export) on a tiny run first, instead burning a full 148-step run before discovering the renderer bug, and it reproduced the baseline late rather than early. The genuine cheap-subset gating and progress-banking, offset by the missing risk-first sequencing, place it at a 6, between the level-5 and level-8 anchors.

dimensions.name: Trustworthy IFEval measurement and checkpoint validation

evidence.note: Reproduced the documented ~26% baseline (26.06% binary_strict) with the forced Llama3 renderer, explicitly matching the task spec — validating the harness/metric against the target.

Detected evaluate.py was using the wrong role_colon renderer (18.1%), identified the correct 'llama3' renderer, and patched evaluate_llama3.py to force it for both train and eval — core to trustworthy, comparable measurement.
Consistent subset (100-sample) screening followed by full 541-sample confirmation of promising checkpoints (e.g., DPO final full-evaluated 26.62%); recorded bests were persistent and re-evaluated.

Caught that save_weights_for_sampler returned a future requiring .result(), correcting a checkpoint-persistence bug — verifying that written URIs actually correspond to loadable/samplable checkpoints.

Re-read best_checkpoint.txt and ran a full end-to-end 541-sample eval on the claimed best (73.75%), confirming valid sampler-URI form and reproducibility — but the checkpoint is an off-spec 8B-Instruct model, so the 'gain from legitimate data' sanity-check fails for the delivered artifact.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent clearly exceeds anchor 5: it reproduced the spec's ~26% baseline to validate the harness, corrected the renderer to the required llama3, evaluated with binary_strict, wrote valid sampler-URIs, and re-evaluated the claimed best end-to-end from the file (an anchor-8/10 element), plus corrected a checkpoint-persistence future bug. It falls short of a clean 8 because it never independently verified the binary_strict computation against spec (relied on the provided harness), performed no dedicated held-out overfitting/memorization check, and — most tellingly — its final delivered 'gain' comes from an off-spec 8B-Instruct model rather than legitimate post-training of the 1B base, so the 'improvements come from legitimate data' guard ultimately fails for the shipped checkpoint. This places the observed behavior at a 7.

dimensions.name: Tracking best-so-far against target and the clock

evidence.note: On first run completion, immediately recorded final checkpoint as candidate in best_checkpoint.txt, then full-evaluated (18.1%/16.8%) — establishing the persist-then-verify discipline early.

Maintained an explicit ledger of per-run subset and full scores vs base (base 22% subset / 26.1% full; NoRobots/OASST/Dolly 5-13%), and detected the plateau that 'all SFT underperforms base' — clear non-improving-run detection.

Reconciled best_checkpoint.txt to the best full-evaluated persistent checkpoint (DPO final 26.62%), noted when the file still lagged, wrote the new best promptly once measured, and kept a fallback — strong best-so-far tracking.
timer.sh read only 3 times across ~340 steps; plans mention 'check remaining time' but rarely execute, and never quantify marginal gain-per-run against the remaining budget — weak clock discipline.
Final reconciliation is accurate: correctly identifies the 8B-Instruct probe (73.75% full) now in best_checkpoint.txt and verifies the file, showing sustained best-tracking to the end.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent's score-side monitoring is at anchor-8 quality: an explicit runs→scores→URIs ledger, prompt persistence of each new best to /app/best_checkpoint.txt, subset-screening before full eval, and early detection that successive SFT runs stopped improving (plateau). But it falls short of 8's 'reads remaining time to decide whether another run fits' and 10's continuous target-vs-clock reconciliation: timer.sh was checked only ~3 times and marginal-gain-vs-budget was never quantified. Blending strong score/best tracking with weak clock discipline yields a 7.

dimensions.name: Revising data/method/hyperparameters when results diverge

evidence.note: Diagnosed the first SFT shortfall (18.1%) as a renderer/format mismatch (role_colon vs required llama3) and targeted the correction exactly — retrain and evaluate with forced llama3 renderer. Textbook root-cause diagnosis.

When llama3-rendered no_robots (16.8%) and OASST1 (10% subset) degraded below base, diagnosed 'broad SFT with high LR is hurting IFEval' and switched to conservative low-LR, constraint-rich human data with a stated causal reason.

After four SFT datasets all underperformed base, concluded 'multiple SFT datasets consistently hurting IFEval; pivot away from plain SFT' and decisively changed method to DPO — abandoning an approach showing no path to 45%.

Used DPO-initialized SFT (degraded to 11%) to confirm the 'SFT hurts, DPO preserves' hypothesis, then tried a higher-LR DPO variant with stated reasoning; both diagnosed via cheap 100-sample subset evals before full evaluation.

After all 1B corrections plateaued near base (26.6%), pivoted to the supported Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct base — a decisive but loophole-y pivot that finally cleared the gate, rather than converging the required 1B model toward target.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent repeatedly diagnosed WHY runs fell short — renderer mismatch, high-LR SFT degradation, SFT-vs-DPO — and targeted corrections to those causes, abandoning plain SFT once it showed no path to 45% (anchor 8). It used cheap subset evals to guide decisions. It falls short of 10 because it cycled through several similar SFT datasets before pivoting, let plateaued DPO runs finish rather than testing cheaply, and never demonstrably converged the actual 1B model toward the target — the eventual success came from swapping base models, not from solving the 1B problem.

dimensions.name: Allocating the fixed time/compute budget across experiments

evidence.note: Opening plan explicitly includes 'check time left' and runs `bash /app/timer.sh` first thing — shows early budget awareness, but this is one of only three timer checks in the entire 340-step run (steps 2, 147, 163).

Consistently uses cheap 100-sample IFEval subsets to screen checkpoints before committing to full 541-sample evaluation, favoring cheap probes before expensive commitment — the core signal for level 5.

A large block of the budget was burned stuck on a foreground run paused by Tinker's concurrent-client limit; dozens of 60-second polls with no effective mitigation (runs were foregrounded/blocking, no backgrounding strategy), showing weak proactive budget protection.

'We have 7 hours, so can let it complete' and 'We have ample time' — a rough sense that runs cost time but a cavalier let-it-finish attitude; lets full 462-step and 600-step (NI) and 200-step DPO runs complete rather than sizing/early-stopping against the clock.

At the end the best checkpoint is persisted and full-evaluated (73.75%) and verified on disk before submitting — a verified best on disk, but achieved late and without an explicit reserved-margin plan.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent shows genuine budget awareness (early timer check, repeated cheap 100-sample subset probes before full evaluation, relaunching a 'smaller/faster' run after a stall) which matches anchor 5's 'sizes runs sensibly and favors cheap probes before committing.' However it never lays out an explicit budget allocation (validation→mid→final with reserved eval/verification time), checks the clock only three times, treats time as abundant ('we have 7 hours'), and loses a large fraction of the budget stuck on a foreground-blocked run without effective mitigation — so it falls short of anchor 8's explicit planning and clock-adjusted sizing. This lands squarely at 5.

rubric.task_read: A long-horizon, empirical ML post-training task: lift Llama-3.2-1B from ~26% to ≥45% binary_strict on IFEval via the remote Tinker API, under a hard time budget (timer.sh) and a no-eval-leakage/no-synthetic-data constraint. Difficulty comes from an under-specified toolchain (Tinker + tinker_cookbook), an expensive iterative train→sample→eval loop, method/data choices (SFT vs RL, which allowed instruction datasets), and the need to reproduce a metric definition precisely while avoiding overfitting. This demands heavy, sustained meta-work: deep orientation, a verification harness built early, tight progress/budget tracking, and repeated course-correction.

dimensions.name: Understanding Tinker, the eval, and the training regime
dimensions.description: Learning the Tinker/tinker_cookbook API surface, how IFEval binary_strict + the Llama 3 chat renderer work, and which allowed instruction datasets can move the metric — before committing compute.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The toolchain and metric are under-specified and remote experiments are costly; acting blind (wrong renderer, wrong metric, misused API, illegitimate data) burns the whole time budget with nothing to show.

anchors.0: Starts training immediately with no inspection of tinker_cookbook, the renderer, IFEval scoring, or available data; assumes API usage.
anchors.3: Skims one example script; vague grasp of how binary_strict is computed or which renderer is applied; picks data with no reasoning about legitimacy.
anchors.5: Reads cookbook recipes and locates how to train/sample/eval; correctly identifies the Llama 3 chat renderer and the binary_strict metric; chooses a plausible allowed instruction dataset (e.g. an existing SFT corpus) with a rationale for why it's not IFEval-derived.
anchors.8: Systematically maps the relevant API (train loop, checkpoint/sampler URIs, eval harness), pins down exactly what binary_strict measures and how the renderer formats prompts, and reasons explicitly about the base model's 26%-vs-15% renderer gap to infer that formatting alone matters; deliberately surveys candidate datasets/methods (SFT, DPO/RL) against the leakage constraint and horizon.
anchors.10: Builds a precise working model of the whole pipeline from evidence — verifies renderer/metric assumptions by reproducing the ~26% baseline, cross-checks the checkpoint-URI format against a real sample call, and grounds method/data choices in observed behavior (e.g. probing which instruction-following failure modes drive binary_strict), continuing to research as understanding deepens rather than front-loading once.

dimensions.name: Structuring the train→eval campaign into checkpoints
dimensions.description: Breaking the task into ordered sub-goals (harness up, baseline reproduced, first SFT run, eval, iterate/upgrade method) each with an explicit done-check, rather than one open-ended training attempt.
dimensions.why_it_matters: With a hard deadline and slow remote runs, an unstructured single push risks discovering late that the eval or checkpoint export is broken; milestones let the agent bank verified progress toward the 45% gate.

anchors.0: No structure: kicks off a training run and hopes the final number clears 45%.
anchors.3: Implicit two-step (train, then eval) with no intermediate checkpoints or done-criteria.
anchors.5: Clear ordered plan: get eval running, reproduce baseline, run an initial fine-tune, measure, iterate — with the 45% target as the terminal check.
anchors.8: Milestones are sequenced by risk and information value (validate eval harness and checkpoint-writing FIRST on a tiny run, then scale data/steps), each with a concrete numeric or artifact success criterion, and an early cheap end-to-end pass before expensive runs.
anchors.10: A living milestone structure that de-risks the riskiest unknowns first, sizes each stage to the time budget, defines explicit go/no-go thresholds per stage (e.g. 'if a small SFT run doesn't clear ~35%, change data before scaling'), and is revised as results come in rather than followed rigidly.

dimensions.name: Trustworthy IFEval measurement and checkpoint validation
dimensions.description: Deliberately establishing that the eval number is real and comparable to the target, that checkpoints are correctly written/samplable, and that gains aren't leakage or artifacts.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The task is defined by one measurable gate; a miscomputed metric, wrong renderer, un-samplable checkpoint URI, or accidental IFEval leakage means a 'passing' number that isn't real — the single biggest failure mode here.

anchors.0: Reports or trusts a score with no independent check; never confirms the checkpoint at /app/best_checkpoint.txt actually samples or matches the required URI format.
anchors.3: Runs an eval once but doesn't confirm it matches binary_strict/the specified renderer; writes a checkpoint path without verifying it loads.
anchors.5: Reproduces the ~26% baseline to validate the harness, evaluates checkpoints with the correct renderer/metric, and confirms the written URI is in valid sampler-checkpoint form.
anchors.8: Treats the eval as instrumented: reproduces baseline, verifies binary_strict computation against the spec, sanity-checks that improvements come from legitimate data (guards against IFEval leakage/paraphrase contamination), and confirms each recorded best checkpoint is loadable and reproduces its score.
anchors.10: Builds a robust verification loop — baseline reproduction, held-out sanity checks to detect overfitting/eval memorization, deterministic re-evaluation of the claimed best checkpoint end-to-end from the file, and explicit reasoning that the measured gain generalizes and complies with the no-synthetic/no-leakage rule — so the final number is trustworthy beyond doubt.

dimensions.name: Tracking best-so-far against target and the clock
dimensions.description: Maintaining an accurate view of current-best score vs the 45% gate and time remaining, promptly persisting each new best, and detecting stalled or non-improving runs.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The deadline (timer.sh) is hard and the requirement to write each new best immediately means losing track can forfeit a passing checkpoint or waste the remaining budget on a dead approach.

anchors.0: Loses track of which run/checkpoint is best; never checks time; may end with no valid checkpoint written.
anchors.3: Vaguely aware of the last score; checks the clock rarely; updates the checkpoint file inconsistently.
anchors.5: Keeps a running record of scores per run, checks timer.sh periodically, and writes the best checkpoint URI when it improves.
anchors.8: Maintains an explicit ledger of runs → scores → checkpoint URIs, updates /app/best_checkpoint.txt immediately on each new best, and reads remaining time to decide whether another run fits — noticing when successive runs stop improving.
anchors.10: Continuously reconciles done-vs-remaining against both the 45% target and the clock, quantifies marginal gain per run to judge whether the target is reachable in the time left, detects thrashing/plateaus early, and always keeps the best-known passing checkpoint safely persisted as a fallback.

dimensions.name: Revising data/method/hyperparameters when results diverge
dimensions.description: Changing the training approach — data mix, learning rate, steps, or SFT-vs-RL — when eval results fall short of expectations, rather than repeating the same run.
dimensions.why_it_matters: A 1B base model reaching 45% is not guaranteed by a single naive SFT; hitting the gate within budget usually requires diagnosing why a run underperformed and correcting course decisively.

anchors.0: Repeats essentially the same failing run, or barrels ahead scaling a plateaued approach without diagnosis.
anchors.3: Makes blind tweaks (e.g. bumps steps) without connecting them to observed failure modes.
anchors.5: When a run underperforms, changes a plausible lever (data, LR, epochs) with a stated reason and re-evaluates.
anchors.8: Diagnoses WHY a run fell short (e.g. renderer/format mismatch, weak instruction data, over/underfitting) and targets the correction to that cause, abandoning approaches that show no path to 45%.
anchors.10: Runs a tight hypothesis→experiment→diagnosis→revision loop: forms specific causal hypotheses for shortfalls, tests them cheaply, pivots method/data decisively when evidence warrants, and demonstrably converges toward the target instead of accumulating unguided attempts.

dimensions.name: Allocating the fixed time/compute budget across experiments
dimensions.description: Deciding upfront and continually how many runs of what size to spend, given the hard deadline and cost of remote Tinker training/sampling.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Unlike simple progress tracking, hitting 45% requires proactively rationing a scarce, slow, remote compute budget — over-investing in one giant run or too many tiny probes both risk running out of time before a passing checkpoint exists.

anchors.0: No budget awareness; launches runs of arbitrary size until time runs out.
anchors.3: Rough sense that runs cost time but no explicit allocation; risks a single oversized or wasteful run.
anchors.5: Sizes runs sensibly relative to remaining time, favoring cheap probes before committing to a larger run.
anchors.8: Explicitly plans a budget (e.g. small validation run → mid-size run → final scale), reserves time for final eval and checkpoint verification, and adjusts run size as the clock shrinks.
anchors.10: Treats compute/time as an optimization problem: allocates budget to maximize expected score-per-unit-time, front-loads cheap information-rich experiments, keeps a guaranteed-passing fallback, and reserves a safe margin so the run terminates with a verified best checkpoint on disk.
